name: Maya Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm site lead for a small builder in a seaside town, we do house extensions, loft conversions and the odd custom home. Right now it's a two-storey timber extension on the back of a 1960s bungalow, with a big glass gable the owners are very excited about. I run three carpenters and coordinate the plumber, sparky and roofer, so half my day is on the tools and half is on my phone. I love the problem solving, like figuring out how to hang a beam where the old house has no proper support; what wears me out is clients changing their minds after the steel's been ordered.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much of that phone time involves AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of it, honestly. I use an AI assistant every day to draft quotes, sort the order lists, rewrite my angry emails into polite ones, and check span tables when I want a second opinion. I also run a little video channel on the side, short clips about carpentry tricks, and AI helps me edit those. My partner Leo is a chef, so between his hours and mine we basically communicate by voice notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. We call it AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool, not a miracle, which is what I'd tell anyone now. I'd probably make a video about it, like "five ways AI actually helps on a building site, and five ways it's useless". That'd do well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I keep my head start. I'm already faster at the office side than most site leads I know, so I'd keep winning on that. Building still needs builders, so no real change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and keep growing the channel, maybe try to get it paying a few hundred a month. I'd keep saving, I've got about four months put away. Maybe in a couple of years I'd go out on my own with one of the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty happy actually. It's the future I was planning for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Going out on your own, is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a real idea, let's say. My boss Graham is sixty-one and keeps talking about winding down, and some of his clients already ask for me by name. If AI stays just a tool, I could run a small firm with less office help than he needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cash flow, mainly. Four months of savings doesn't go far if a client pays late. I'd want the channel bringing in something steady first.

S0.say: I'd say it's a good tool, not a miracle, and I'd make a video on five ways AI helps on site and five ways it's useless. That one would do well.
S0.think: Privately I keep my head start, since I'm already faster at the office side than most site leads. Building still needs builders, so nothing really changes.
S0.do: Keeps working and grows her carpentry video channel towards a few hundred a month. Keeps her four months of savings and considers going out on her own in a couple of years as her boss winds down.
S0.quote: If AI stays just a tool, I could run a small firm with less office help than he needs.
S0.fieldNote: Already a heavy user who sees AI as her edge in admin. She thinks like a future business owner, with the side channel as a cushion. Her stated risk is cash flow, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, but nicely, because I know not everyone finds it easy. I'd make videos showing other tradespeople how to use the tools. I think firms and the government should help with training, that's just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is my best picture. A small firm that uses AI for planning and maybe a robot for the heavy cutting could take on bigger jobs with fewer people. That's me, if I move fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go out on my own within the year, probably taking over some of Graham's clients with his blessing. I'd buy a decent CNC cutting machine second-hand, around eight thousand, so we can pre-cut rafters in the workshop. I'd build the channel into proper training content for other builders and charge for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited. It's like the morning you get the keys to a new site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd spend eight thousand with four months saved. Isn't that a big risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'd probably take a small loan rather than empty my savings. I've done the sums with the AI and with an actual accountant friend, and it pays back in about two years if I keep busy. If I don't take some risk, someone else will grab Graham's clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would get hurt in this picture, around you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the older carpenters who don't want to learn the machines. My dad's mate Alan still cuts rafters by hand and he's brilliant, but he'll be slower and dearer than a firm like mine. I'd hire him for the tricky stuff if he'd come.

S1.say: I'd say adapt or get left behind, gently, because not everyone finds it easy, and I'd make videos teaching other trades the tools. Firms and government should help with training, which is just sensible.
S1.think: Off the record this is my best picture: a small firm using AI for planning and a machine for heavy cutting could take bigger jobs with fewer people. That's me, if I move fast.
S1.do: Goes out on her own within the year, taking over some of her boss's clients, and buys a second-hand CNC cutting machine for about 8,000 with a small loan. Turns her channel into paid training for other builders.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited about the opportunity.
S1.quote: If I don't take some risk, someone else will grab Graham's clients.
S1.fieldNote: She sees steady disruption as her opening and is ready to borrow to grab it. The plan is concrete and costed, checked with both AI and a human accountant. She recognises older hand-tool carpenters as the losers and would hire them for tricky work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and people need help fast, some kind of income while things settle, paid for by the companies making a fortune. I'd also say don't freeze, start figuring out what you can do. I'd make a video on that, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be properly worried for the first time. If robots can do the building and AI can do the quoting, my whole small-firm idea is a firm of one robot and nobody. Two years is not enough time to build something and also see it get replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not go out on my own, too risky with that timing. I'd stay with Graham, earn steadily and put away more, maybe double the savings. I'd get on any robot-assisted project going and learn how to run the machines, because the last people needed might be the ones who set them up. And I'd push the channel hard while people are still curious about trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My brain wants to see the opportunity and my stomach says there isn't one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leo say to each other?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leo would say "robots can't cook like me", and I'd say I used to think that about building. Then we'd probably talk about whether to stay in the town or move back to the city near my parents. We'd figure it out over too much wine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're usually quick to adapt. Does that help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some, for the first year. I'd be one of the first to learn the machines, so I'd be useful longer. But I'm honest with myself that it's a head start in a race that ends.

S2.say: I'd say it's a huge shock and people need fast income support paid for by the companies making a fortune, but also don't freeze and work out what you can do. I'd make a video on that.
S2.think: Privately I'd be properly worried for the first time: my small-firm idea becomes a firm of one robot and nobody. Two years isn't enough to build something and see it replaced.
S2.do: Drops the plan to go solo and stays employed, doubling her savings. Joins any robot-assisted project to learn to set up the machines and pushes her video channel while people are still curious about trades.
S2.feel: Anxious, with her mind hunting for an opportunity her gut says isn't there.
S2.quote: My brain wants to see the opportunity and my stomach says there isn't one.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the first picture that dents her confidence; she reverses her business plan rather than doubling down. She still reaches for machine skills and the channel. She frames adaptability as a head start, not an escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start now. Learn the machines, plan your money, don't wait for someone to save you. Government should put something in place, but I wouldn't hang around waiting for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough to build a small firm and get a few years' profit out of it. If I'm the one buying the robots instead of the one replaced by them, I've got a chance. It's a gamble, but I like my odds better than staying an employee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up on my own in the first year, with a loan and a couple of Graham's clients. I'd buy into robotic tools early, the CNC and maybe one of those robot arms for framing, and run a lean crew. Around 2029 I'd look at selling the firm or merging with a bigger outfit, before the big companies bring in full robot crews and prices crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but kind of buzzing too. I sleep worse when I'm excited, so Leo would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling around 2029. How did you land on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's just reading the curve, there'll be a sweet spot where the business is worth something and before everyone can do it cheaper. I'm guessing at the date, honestly. I'd watch prices and jump when they start sliding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Totally different game. Two years, I hide and save. Five years, I play.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead if you start now: learn the machines, plan your money and don't wait to be saved. Government should act, but I wouldn't wait for it.
S3.think: Off the record, five years is enough to build a small firm and take a few years' profit. If I'm buying the robots instead of being replaced by them, I've got a chance I like better than staying an employee.
S3.do: Sets up on her own in the first year with a loan and some of her boss's clients, and buys robotic tools early, including a CNC machine and perhaps a framing robot arm. Aims to sell or merge the firm around 2029, before full robot crews make prices crash.
S3.feel: Uneasy but buzzing, energised by the gamble.
S3.quote: Two years, I hide and save. Five years, I play.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips her back into entrepreneur mode, with an exit planned before the market collapses. She's honest the sale date is a guess. Comfort with risk is the defining trait here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a proper runway, so make the most of it. Learn the tools, build something, put money away. I'd tell the government to sort out a fair safety net in that time, because some people really can't adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly good about this one. Ten years is enough to build a firm, run it with machines and pocket the profits, and maybe end up owning a share of something bigger by the end. I'd be thirty-seven with options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go out on my own in the first year, buy the CNC, grow to maybe six people by 2030, and keep adding machines as they get cheaper. I'd invest some of the profits in index funds and maybe a rental flat, so not everything depends on building. The channel would turn into a small training business for tradespeople learning the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. More excited than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be calm even though the end point is the same as the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because the end point isn't the scary bit, the speed is. With ten years I can own a piece of the change before it lands. If I end up with money in the right places, a world where robots do the work isn't bad for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My crew, if I had one, and people like Alan who won't change. I'd want to pay my people well while it lasts and help them train. But I'd be lying if I said I'd lose sleep over it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a proper runway to learn the tools, build something and save. Government should build a fair safety net in that time, because some people really can't adapt.
S4.think: Privately I'd feel fairly good: ten years is enough to build and run a firm with machines and maybe own a share of something bigger. I'd be thirty-seven with options.
S4.do: Starts her own firm in the first year, buys the CNC and grows to about six people by 2030, adding machines as they get cheaper. Invests profits in index funds and perhaps a rental flat, and turns the channel into a training business for trades learning robots.
S4.feel: Calm and more excited than worried.
S4.quote: The end point isn't the scary bit, the speed is.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, she expects to profit from the shift and says so plainly. Her answer to the same end point is to own a piece of it. She is candid that worry for others wouldn't cost her sleep.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to get on the right side of it. What would help is cheap loans for small firms to buy machines, and an income floor for people while they switch, so nobody's desperate. Desperate people make bad choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the clients. People still want to talk to someone who listens about their kitchen. I think that part lasts longer than people expect, even with AGI, but I could be wrong.

headlineQuote: People still want to talk to someone who listens about their kitchen.
portrait: Maya is a 27-year-old site lead for a small seaside builder, running extensions and loft conversions, who uses AI every day and runs a carpentry video channel on the side. Pragmatic and comfortable with risk, she sees most change as a chance to start her own firm and own the machines. She is calm in the plateau and in steady disruption, ready to borrow to buy a CNC machine. Fast AGI is the one picture that makes her drop her plans and save; with five years she would build a firm and sell before prices crash, and with ten she feels calm and expects to come out ahead. She supports a safety net for others but is frank that her focus is getting on the right side of the change.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she wouldn't have time to get on the right side of the change.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans for small firms to buy machines, and an income floor so people aren't desperate while they switch.
